newsitem.title: INDIA: India oil pool deficit needs addressing - ministry.
newsitem.headline: India oil pool deficit needs addressing - ministry.

text.p: Indian Finance Secretary Montek Singh Ahluwalia said on Saturday that the government had taken note of a mounting oil subsidy bill but not addressed the problem in the 1997/98 (April-March) budget.
"The oil pool deficit is a problem but it is not expected to be met from budgetary allocation," Ahluwalia, the highest ranking civil servant in the Finance Ministry, told a news conference.
The oil pool deficit, estimated at 155 billion rupees ($4.3 billion), is the amount the government owes oil companies for selling petroleum products to Indian consumers way below world prices.
Ahluwalia said the issue was being debated in parliament.

He said President Shankar Dayal Sharma had noted the problem in a speech to parliament last month when he said: "Healthy development of the oil sector in the country demands that the oil pool account is in balance."

That remark, cleared in advance by Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's government, was widely intepreted as a sign that the ruling coalition was planning to raise petroleum product prices to reduce the oil pool deficit.
But no price rise was included in the budget which was presented to parliament on Friday.
"This is a deficit which has to be taken care of, but it did not come up in the budget," Ahluwalia said. "The deficit has to be sorted out by the petroleum sector.
Asked about the possibility of dismantling oil price subsidies, Ahluwalia said it was a matter for the Petroleum Ministry.
Ahluwalia said that although the budget did not directly address the oil pool deficit, it did provide new incentives to oil firms for exploration.
"Major incentives are provided for domestic crude oil exploration in the budget," he said.

Finance Minister P. Chidambaram said on Friday the budget provided for a new exploration licensing policy. Firms including state-controlled Oil and Natural Gas Corp (ONGC) and Oil India Ltd (OIL), would be paid the international price of oil for new discoveries.
The domestic firms would get the same duty concessions on imports of capital goods as private production-sharing contracts, Chidambaram added.
